b2.title: What Happens When We Sleep
b2.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 B2 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep a night, yet many regularly get far less. Sleep is not simply a pause in our day. While we rest, the brain moves through several stages, including REM sleep, when most vivid dreaming takes place.

These stages play an important role in memory. During deep sleep, the brain appears to strengthen the connections formed during the day, which helps us hold on to new information. Missing out on sleep, on the other hand, can affect our mood, our concentration and even our appetite.

One common obstacle is screen time before bed. Bright light from phones can delay the release of melatonin, a hormone that tells the body it is time to sleep. Experts suggest keeping a regular bedtime and switching devices off well before you turn out the light.

b2.title: The Secret Life of a Bee Colony
b2.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 B2 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: A honey bee colony works like a small, well-organized city. Each hive usually has one queen, whose main job is to lay eggs, along with thousands of female worker bees and a smaller number of males called drones.

Worker bees take on different tasks as they get older, from cleaning the hive to collecting nectar and pollen. When a bee finds a good source of food, it returns home and performs a "waggle dance" that tells the others which direction to fly and roughly how far to go.

Bees matter far beyond the hive. By carrying pollen from flower to flower, they pollinate many of the fruits and vegetables we eat. However, bee populations face serious threats, including pesticides, parasites and the loss of the wild flowers they depend on.

b2.title: Why Most Plastic Is Never Recycled
b2.zh: 為什麼大部分塑膠沒有被回收
b2.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 B2 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: We often throw plastic bottles into the recycling bin and assume the problem is solved. In reality, only a small share of all the plastic ever produced has been recycled. Much of it ends up in landfills, is burned, or leaks into rivers and oceans.

Part of the difficulty is that plastic comes in many different types. Items are usually marked with a number from one to seven. Bottles made of PET (number 1) and containers made of HDPE (number 2) are the easiest to recycle, while many others are rarely accepted.

Dirty or mixed materials cause further problems, because food waste can contaminate a whole batch. Even when plastic is recycled, it is often turned into lower-quality products. That is why many experts argue that using less plastic in the first place matters most.

b2.title: Thirty Days to Try Something New

source.name: TED：Matt Cutts, Try something new for 30 days

b2.note: 內容主題取自 TED 熱門演講。內文為學習用改寫，不是講者原話，請看原演講了解細節。
paras: In his short TED talk, Google engineer Matt Cutts describes a simple idea that changed his life. Feeling stuck in a routine, he decided to try something new for 30 days. Thirty days, he explains, is just about the right amount of time to add a new habit or remove an old one.

The experiments ranged from biking to work to taking a picture every day. Over time, he noticed that the months became far more memorable. His self-confidence grew too, and he eventually climbed Mount Kilimanjaro and wrote a novel of 50,000 words in a single month.

Cutts also observes that small, sustainable changes are more likely to stick than big, dramatic ones. His challenge to the audience is easy to accept: think of something you have always wanted to try, and give it the next 30 days.

c1.title: The Hidden Work of a Sleeping Brain
c1.zh: 大腦在睡眠中默默做的事
c1.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 C1 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: Sleep is easily dismissed as wasted time, yet the brain is anything but idle at night. Over the course of a typical night, it cycles several times through distinct stages, from light and deep non-REM sleep to REM sleep, the phase most closely associated with vivid dreaming.

Each stage appears to serve a purpose. Deep sleep is thought to consolidate memories, transferring fragile new information into more durable storage, while REM sleep may help us process emotions. Cut these cycles short, and the effects quickly surface in poorer attention, irritability and impaired judgment.

Chronic sleep loss carries subtler costs as well. It has been linked to changes in the hormones that regulate hunger, which may partly explain why tired people crave sugary food, and to a weaker immune response.

Modern habits rarely help. Exposure to bright screens late in the evening can suppress melatonin and push back the body's internal clock. The remedy is unglamorous but effective: a consistent schedule, a dark and quiet bedroom, and a firm cut-off time for devices.

c1.title: How a Hive Thinks Without a Leader
c1.zh: 沒有領袖的蜂巢如何做決定
c1.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 C1 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: It is tempting to imagine the queen as the ruler of a honey bee colony, but she gives no orders. Her role is chiefly reproductive. The daily running of the hive emerges instead from the actions of tens of thousands of workers, each responding to simple signals from its surroundings.

The division of labor is strikingly flexible. Young workers tend the brood and build wax comb; older ones graduate to foraging. Foragers that locate a rich patch of flowers communicate its position through the waggle dance, encoding direction relative to the sun and distance in the length of each run.
The ecological stakes are considerable. Bees pollinate a large proportion of the crops humans rely on, from almonds to apples, so a decline in their numbers reverberates through the food system.

That decline is not driven by a single culprit. Pesticides, parasitic mites, disease and the disappearance of wildflower habitats all combine to weaken colonies, which is why protecting bees calls for changes in farming, not just in beekeeping.

c1.title: The Limits of Recycling Plastic
c1.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 C1 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: Few habits feel as virtuous as rinsing out a bottle and dropping it in the recycling bin. Yet the comforting image of an endless loop is largely an illusion: only a small fraction of all the plastic ever manufactured has actually been recycled, while the rest has been landfilled, incinerated or lost to the environment.

The obstacles are partly chemical. Plastics are a family of very different materials, flagged by resin codes from one to seven, and they cannot simply be melted down together. Only a few, notably PET drinks bottles and HDPE containers, have reliable markets.

Contamination compounds the problem. A single greasy food tray can spoil an entire bale, and even clean material tends to degrade with each round of processing. As a result, recycling often means downcycling into lower-grade products that will not be recycled again.

None of this makes recycling pointless, but it does shift the emphasis. Many researchers now argue that the most effective strategies lie further upstream: designing products with fewer materials, expanding reuse systems and simply producing less plastic to begin with.

c1.title: The Case for Thirty-Day Experiments

source.name: TED：Matt Cutts, Try something new for 30 days

c1.note: 內容主題取自 TED 熱門演講。內文為學習用改寫，不是講者原話，請看原演講了解細節。
paras: Matt Cutts, then an engineer at Google, opens his brief TED talk with a confession: he had fallen into a rut. Borrowing an idea from the filmmaker Morgan Spurlock, he resolved to try something new for 30 days, a span he considers long enough to form or break a habit without becoming daunting.

The challenges themselves were modest at first, such as cycling to work or taking a photograph each day. What surprised him was the cumulative effect. Instead of blurring together, the months became distinct and memorable.

As one experiment led to another, his confidence grew. He found himself climbing Mount Kilimanjaro and, during one November, writing a 50,000-word novel. He admits it was not a masterpiece, but finishing it still mattered to him.

b2.title: How Much Water Do We Really Need?
b2.zh: 我們到底需要喝多少水？
b2.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 B2 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: Water makes up around 60 percent of an adult's body, and we lose some of it every day through breathing, sweating and going to the toilet. Replacing that water is essential for controlling body temperature and keeping our organs working properly.

You may have heard that everyone should drink eight glasses a day, but this rule is not based on strong scientific evidence. How much you need depends on your size, how active you are and the climate you live in. A surprising amount also comes from food, especially fruit and vegetables.

Early signs of dehydration include thirst, headaches and dark yellow urine. For many people around the world, the bigger problem is access: roughly two billion people still do not have a reliable supply of safe drinking water at home.

b2.title: Why More Cities Are Choosing Bikes

paras: In cities such as Amsterdam and Copenhagen, the bicycle is not just a hobby but a normal way to get to work, school and the shops. Cycling for everyday trips like these is known as utility cycling, and more cities are trying to encourage it.

The benefits are easy to see. Bikes take up little space, produce no exhaust fumes and give riders regular exercise. For short journeys in busy areas, they are often quicker than cars stuck in traffic.

However, people will only switch to cycling if they feel safe. That is why successful cities invest in protected bike lanes, secure parking and public bike-sharing systems like Taiwan's YouBike. Electric bikes are also making longer or hillier trips possible for many riders.

b2.title: Can You Tell If a Photo Is Fake?
b2.zh: 你分得出照片是假的嗎？

paras: AI tools can now create realistic photos of events that never happened. In his TED talk, Hany Farid, a professor who has spent decades studying digital images, explains how experts try to tell real pictures from fake ones.

Some clues are hidden in the physics of the scene. In a real photo, shadows and parallel lines follow consistent rules, while AI-generated images often get these details slightly wrong. Experts also study tiny patterns of noise in the image that ordinary viewers cannot see.

Farid warns that most of us cannot reliably spot fakes with our own eyes. His advice is to slow down before sharing something shocking, check where it came from and rely on trustworthy sources. Avoiding becoming part of the problem, he suggests, is something everyone can do.

c1.title: Beyond Eight Glasses a Day
c1.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 C1 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: Water accounts for roughly 60 percent of an adult's body weight, and it is in constant circulation: we shed it with every breath, every bead of sweat and every trip to the bathroom. Keeping that balance steady is fundamental to regulating temperature, transporting nutrients and allowing the kidneys to clear waste.

Popular advice tends to boil down to a tidy formula: eight glasses a day. The figure is easy to remember but has surprisingly little evidence behind it. Actual requirements fluctuate with body size, activity and climate, and a substantial share of our intake arrives through food.

For healthy people, thirst is generally a dependable guide, although older adults may not feel it as keenly. Mild dehydration tends to announce itself through headaches, fatigue and darker urine long before it becomes dangerous.

Globally, however, the more pressing issue is not how much people drink but whether what they drink is safe. Around two billion people still lack safely managed drinking water, which leaves them exposed to preventable diseases and makes clean water as much a question of justice as of health.

c1.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 C1 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: In Amsterdam or Copenhagen, it is unremarkable to see office workers in suits, parents with children perched on cargo bikes and pensioners laden with shopping, all pedaling through rush hour. This is utility cycling: the bike treated as transport rather than sport.

Its appeal to city planners is easy to grasp. Bicycles occupy a fraction of the road space of cars, emit nothing at the tailpipe and build physical activity into daily routines. Over short distances in congested centers, they frequently beat motor traffic door to door.

Yet these cities did not stumble into cycling by accident; they engineered it. Decades of investment produced networks of protected lanes, secure parking and traffic-calmed streets that make riding feel safe even for nervous beginners.

That lesson travels. Surveys consistently show that perceived danger, not distance, is what keeps would-be cyclists off their bikes. Public bike-sharing schemes such as Taiwan's YouBike lower the barrier further, while electric bikes are rapidly widening the range of journeys that cycling can realistically replace.

c1.title: Seeing Is No Longer Believing

source.name: TED：Hany Farid, How to spot fake AI photos

c1.note: 內容主題取自 TED 熱門演講。內文為學習用改寫，不是講者原話，請看原演講了解細節。
paras: Generative AI has made it trivial to produce photographs of events that never took place, and the consequences reach from personal reputations to public trust. Hany Farid, a professor who has spent his career in digital forensics, uses his TED talk to show how specialists fight back.

Much of the evidence lies in physics that image generators only imitate. In a genuine photograph, parallel lines converge on a consistent vanishing point and shadows align with a single light source. Synthetic images frequently break these rules in ways that become obvious once measured.

Other tests probe what the eye cannot see at all, such as the statistical fingerprint of sensor noise that a camera leaves behind. Farid is candid, though, that ordinary viewers cannot rely on intuition, and that detection is an arms race rather than a solved problem.

c1.title: The Moon's Quiet Influence on Earth
c1.zh: 月球對地球默默的影響
c1.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 C1 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: Hanging some 384,000 kilometers away, the Moon can seem like little more than a decorative feature of the night sky. In fact, it is intimately bound up with Earth's history and present-day behavior.

The prevailing theory holds that it coalesced around 4.5 billion years ago from debris thrown out when a Mars-sized body struck the infant Earth. Over time, tidal forces slowed its rotation until it became tidally locked, which is why the same hemisphere perpetually faces us.

Those same forces govern the ocean tides, shaping coastal ecosystems and, over geological time, gradually lengthening our day. The Moon also helps stabilize the tilt of Earth's axis, which some scientists believe has kept our climate more stable than it might otherwise have been.

Only twelve people, all Apollo astronauts between 1969 and 1972, have ever set foot there. Yet after a half-century hiatus, the Moon is back on the agenda, with space agencies now aiming to return crews and, eventually, to establish a sustained presence on its surface.

From the Arabian Peninsula, the drink traveled along trade routes into the Ottoman Empire, where coffeehouses flourished, and then into Europe.

There they acquired a reputation as hotbeds of conversation and commerce; some London coffeehouses evolved into institutions that still shape finance today. Authorities occasionally tried to suppress them, suspecting that so much animated discussion might breed dissent.

What we call beans are the seeds of coffee cherries, mostly from arabica and robusta plants. Even the much-quoted goal of 10,000 daily steps has humble commercial origins. It traces back to a 1960s Japanese marketing campaign for a pedometer, not to any clinical trial. More recent research suggests that substantial benefits accrue at considerably lower counts, and that any increase over a sedentary baseline is worthwhile.
The rewards are wide-ranging. Brisk, regular walking improves cardiovascular fitness, helps regulate blood sugar and is associated with lower rates of depression.

There is a cognitive dividend too. In a Stanford study, participants generated markedly more creative ideas while walking than while seated, an effect that lingered even after they sat back down. paras: Julian Treasure, who studies sound and communication, opens his TED talk with a question that will resonate with anyone who has been talked over in a meeting: why do some voices command attention while others are ignored?

His answer starts with what he calls the deadly sins of speaking, habits that quietly erode a listener's goodwill. Gossip, judging, negativity, complaining, excuses, embellishment and dogmatism all make people tune out, regardless of how eloquent the speaker may be.

b2.title: What Makes a Typhoon So Powerful?

paras: Typhoons are tropical cyclones, giant spinning storms that form over warm ocean water. The same kind of storm is called a hurricane in the Atlantic and a typhoon in the northwest Pacific, which is why Taiwan uses the second name.

The storms draw their energy from warm seawater, usually at least 26 degrees Celsius. As the warm, wet air rises, it releases heat that makes the winds even stronger. At the center is the eye, a surprisingly calm area surrounded by the most violent winds.

Strong winds are only one danger. Heavy rain can cause floods and landslides, especially in mountain areas, and rising seawater can flood the coast. When a warning is issued, it is wise to stay indoors, prepare water and food, and follow official instructions.

c1.title: Rethinking the 'Lungs of the Earth'
c1.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 C1 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: Tropical rainforests occupy a modest share of the planet's land surface, yet they harbor more than half of its terrestrial species. The Amazon alone sprawls across nine countries and contains a staggering variety of life, much of it still undocumented.

The popular label 'lungs of the Earth' is evocative but scientifically shaky. A mature forest does generate vast quantities of oxygen through photosynthesis, but its own organisms consume nearly all of it, so its net contribution to the air we breathe is close to zero.
The forest's true planetary value lies elsewhere: in the enormous stores of carbon locked in its trees and soils, and in the moisture it recycles into rainfall across entire continents.

That is why deforestation is so consequential. Clearing land for cattle pasture, soy and palm oil not only destroys habitats but also releases stored carbon, turning a buffer against climate change into a contributor to it. c1.title: What Science Says About Learning a Language as an Adult
c1.zh: 科學怎麼看成年人學語言
c1.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 C1 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: The belief that adults are hopeless language learners is remarkably persistent, and only partly justified. Children who are immersed early do tend to achieve a more native-like accent, but in controlled comparisons adults often progress faster in the initial stages, drawing on mature reasoning and better study habits.

A highly influential idea in the field holds that acquisition is driven by comprehensible input: language we can mostly understand, pitched slightly beyond our current level. Exposure of this kind lets learners absorb grammar implicitly, as patterns rather than memorized rules.
Consistency, meanwhile, tends to outperform intensity. Spaced review, in which words resurface at gradually lengthening intervals, exploits the way memory consolidates over time.

Genuine interaction forces us to retrieve and adapt what we know under pressure. Perhaps the most decisive factor, though, is motivation. Learners who tie the language to a meaningful personal goal, whether a career, a relationship or a love of the culture, are far more likely to persevere through the inevitable plateaus.

c1.title: Anatomy of a Typhoon

paras: A typhoon is a mature tropical cyclone, a vast rotating system that can span hundreds of kilometers. The phenomenon is identical to an Atlantic hurricane; only the name changes with geography, and in the northwest Pacific, including the waters around Taiwan, 'typhoon' is the convention.

These storms are essentially heat engines. They typically require sea-surface temperatures of at least 26 degrees Celsius. As moist air ascends and condenses into towering clouds, it releases latent heat, which lowers surface pressure and draws in yet more air, sustaining a self-reinforcing cycle.
At the core lies the eye, an eerily tranquil zone of sinking air ringed by the eyewall, where winds are at their most ferocious.

For Taiwan, the gravest hazards are often not the winds themselves but the water. Torrential rain on steep, saturated slopes can trigger landslides and flash floods, while storm surges inundate low-lying coasts. paras: Tim Urban, the writer behind the blog Wait But Why, opens his TED talk with a sheepish confession: as a student, he postponed a 90-page thesis until the final 72 hours and then produced it in a frenzy of all-nighters.

c1.title: The Real Climate Math of Electric Cars

c1.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 C1 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: Electric vehicles have moved from novelty to mainstream with remarkable speed, now accounting for a sizable share of new car sales worldwide. Their most obvious advantage is local: with no tailpipe, they eliminate exhaust emissions on the street, improving urban air quality and reducing noise.

Their climate credentials, however, depend heavily on context. An electric car's lifetime footprint hinges on the carbon intensity of the grid that charges it, and manufacturing its battery is energy-intensive, so an EV typically starts life with a larger carbon debt than a comparable petrol car.

Lifecycle analyses nonetheless find that this debt is usually repaid within a few years of driving, after which the electric car pulls steadily ahead. As grids add more renewable power, the margin widens further.

Challenges remain. Mining lithium, cobalt and nickel raises environmental and human-rights concerns, prompting interest in recycling and alternative chemistries. And range anxiety, the fear of running out of charge, still deters some buyers, even as longer-range batteries and denser charging networks steadily erode its basis.

A growing body of research suggests the exchange is more reciprocal than it appears. Regular volunteers tend to report greater life satisfaction, lower levels of loneliness and a stronger sense of purpose. Some describe a burst of well-being dubbed the 'helper's high'.

Studies of older adults have even linked volunteering with better physical health, although it is difficult to disentangle cause from effect, since healthier people may simply be more able to volunteer.

Good intentions are not sufficient on their own, however. Well-meaning efforts can backfire when volunteers lack relevant skills or arrive without understanding local needs, a criticism often leveled at short-term 'voluntourism' abroad. The most effective volunteers tend to commit consistently to a cause they care about, through organizations accountable to the communities they serve.

paras: In this hugely popular TED talk, Simon Sinek asks why some leaders and companies inspire people while others do not. His answer is a simple idea he calls the Golden Circle, made of three rings: Why, How and What.

paras: Simon Sinek's talk on the Golden Circle has become a staple of leadership seminars, largely because it offers a compact answer to a puzzling question: why do some organizations and leaders command loyalty while equally capable competitors do not?

His model consists of three concentric rings. Every organization knows what it does, and many know how, but surprisingly few can articulate why they exist beyond making money. Sinek contends that inspiring leaders communicate from the inside out, leading with conviction and letting products serve as proof of that belief.
He illustrates the point with Apple, whose marketing foregrounds a challenge to the status quo, and with the Wright brothers, who were driven by purpose rather than by money or prestige.

c1.title: Why Libraries Still Matter in a Digital Age

paras: When almost any fact can be summoned on a phone in seconds, the public library might seem destined for obsolescence. Instead, many libraries are thriving, having reinvented themselves around what the internet cannot easily supply.

Their collections now extend well beyond print. Patrons borrow e-books and audiobooks, use free computers and Wi-Fi, attend workshops on everything from coding to tax returns, and experiment in makerspaces equipped with 3D printers and tools.
For people without reliable home internet, these services are not a convenience but a lifeline for job applications, schoolwork and government forms.

Yet the library's most distinctive role may be social rather than informational. It is one of the last indoor public spaces where anyone may linger without being expected to buy anything. Sociologists sometimes call such places 'social infrastructure', and their value becomes conspicuous when they disappear: isolated older people, students seeking quiet and parents with small children all lose a shared, neutral ground.

c1.title: The True Price of Convenience
c1.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 C1 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: In barely three decades, e-commerce has evolved from a curiosity into an infrastructure we take for granted. Amazon began in the mid-1990s by selling books online; today, a few taps can summon almost anything to the doorstep within days, sometimes within hours.

The benefits for consumers are genuine. Price comparison is effortless, reviews reduce the risk of a bad purchase and people with limited mobility gain access to goods they might struggle to reach. In Taiwan, collecting parcels at ubiquitous convenience stores has made the system remarkably efficient.
The costs, however, are largely externalized. Rapid delivery fragments shipments into countless small packages, multiplying cardboard and plastic waste and adding delivery vans to congested streets.

Generous free-return policies encourage shoppers to order several sizes and send most back, and a share of those returns is cheaper to discard than to restock. Meanwhile, interfaces engineered to minimize friction make impulse purchases almost effortless. c1.title: Daring to Be Seen

paras: Brené Brown introduces herself as a researcher who prefers what can be measured, which makes the subject of her famous TED talk all the more striking. After years of collecting stories about connection, she kept encountering shame, the fear that something about us makes us unworthy of connection.

Sorting her data, she identified a group she calls the 'wholehearted': people with a strong sense of love and belonging. What set them apart was not luck or status but the conviction that they were worthy of it. b2.title: Why Music Moves Us

b2.title: Can Body Language Change How We Feel?

c1.title: The Urban Forest as Infrastructure
c1.zh: 把城市森林當作基礎建設

paras: On a summer afternoon, a dense city center can be several degrees hotter than the surrounding countryside. Concrete, asphalt and glass soak up solar energy by day and radiate it after dark, while traffic and air conditioners add waste heat of their own. Climatologists call this the urban heat island effect.

Trees counteract it through two mechanisms. Their canopies intercept sunlight before it reaches pavements and walls, and transpiration, the evaporation of water from leaves, draws heat from the surrounding air. A well-shaded street can feel markedly cooler than an exposed one nearby.
Their benefits extend further: root systems absorb stormwater that would otherwise overwhelm drains, and exposure to greenery has been associated with lower stress.

Planners increasingly treat this canopy as infrastructure rather than decoration, yet it is often unevenly distributed. Wealthier districts frequently enjoy far more tree cover than poorer ones, compounding health inequalities as heatwaves intensify. Correcting that imbalance requires sustained investment, and choosing species suited to cramped streets and a changing climate.

Neuroscientists have traced some of music's hold on us to the brain's reward system. In a well-known study, listeners' brains released dopamine at the emotional peak of their favorite pieces. Intriguingly, there was also a surge in the moments of anticipation beforehand, suggesting that part of the pleasure lies in predicting where the music is heading.
This deep integration makes music clinically useful. Music therapy is employed to ease pain and anxiety.

Strikingly, people with advanced dementia sometimes recall and sing songs from their youth long after other memories have faded. For children, sustained instrumental training has been linked to sharper auditory processing, although claims that it broadly raises intelligence remain contested.

Taiwan's High Speed Rail, inaugurated in 2007, illustrates the appeal. Running at up to 300 kilometers per hour along the island's populous western corridor, its fastest trains connect Taipei and Kaohsiung in roughly an hour and a half, effectively turning the length of the island into a day trip and reshaping commuting patterns.
The environmental case is compelling: per passenger, electric trains generally emit far less carbon than planes, and they deliver travelers directly into city centers rather than distant airports.

The economics are more delicate. Dedicated tracks, tunnels and viaducts entail enormous upfront costs, and ridership must be high to justify them. The sweet spot tends to be dense corridors linking major cities a few hundred kilometers apart, close enough to beat flying door to door, far enough to beat driving.

c1.title: Power Poses and the Replication Debate
c1.zh: 權力姿勢與再現性爭議

source.name: TED：Amy Cuddy, Your body language may shape who you are

c1.note: 內容主題取自 TED 熱門演講。內文為學習用改寫，不是講者原話，請看原演講了解細節。
paras: Amy Cuddy's 2012 TED talk on body language became one of the most viewed in the platform's history, partly because its promise was so accessible. Observing that across species, dominance is expressed by expanding the body and submission by shrinking it, she asked whether the influence could run in reverse.

Her answer, based on an early study, was that holding an expansive 'power pose' for two minutes might not only make people feel more powerful but also shift hormone levels. She urged viewers, especially those who felt marginalized, to try it before stressful encounters.

The subsequent story has become a case study in scientific self-correction. Larger replication attempts failed to reproduce the hormonal effects, and one of Cuddy's co-authors publicly distanced herself from the findings, igniting a fierce debate about research methods.

Yet the picture is not wholly negative. A number of later analyses suggest that posture can modestly influence how powerful people report feeling, even if broader behavioral and physiological claims lack robust support. The episode is a useful reminder that a compelling talk and a settled finding are not the same thing.

b2.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 B2 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。

Controlled trials in adults have generally failed to show that breakfast in itself aids weight control.

c1.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 C1 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: It is natural to assume that laughter is primarily a response to humor, but people who study it closely paint a different picture. In naturalistic observations, much laughter follows remarks that are not remotely funny, such as greetings or mundane comments, suggesting that its main function is social rather than comedic.

That interpretation is reinforced by how strongly laughter depends on company. People laugh far more often in conversation than in solitude, and laughter is famously contagious, spreading through a group almost involuntarily.

Many researchers see it as an ancient signal of safety and affiliation, with parallels in the playful panting of apes. Physiologically, a bout of genuine laughter is associated with the release of endorphins, which may account for the sense of warmth and the modest rise in pain tolerance it can produce.

Laughter also defuses tension and signals that a potential conflict is not serious. Seen this way, a shared laugh is less a reaction to a punchline than a brief act of bonding, one that binds a group together long after the joke is forgotten.

The surrounding Yushan National Park spans an extraordinary range of habitats in a short distance, from subtropical forest to alpine scrub. Returning to graduate school in psychology, she examined people in very different high-stakes settings, from cadets at West Point to contestants in the National Spelling Bee and novice teachers in tough schools. paras: A remarkable share of our daily behavior unfolds without deliberate thought. Once an action has been repeated often enough in a stable context, control gradually shifts toward brain circuits that specialize in automatic routines, freeing attention for other demands. This efficiency is a gift, but it also explains why bad habits are so stubborn.

A widely popularized model breaks habits into a loop: a cue, such as a time, place or emotion, prompts a routine, which is reinforced by a reward. c1.title: The Science and Limits of Forecasting

paras: A modern weather forecast is the product of an immense global collaboration. Every day, surface stations, weather balloons, ships, commercial aircraft, radar and satellites gather millions of measurements of temperature, pressure, humidity and wind, which are shared across national meteorological services.

Those observations initialize numerical weather prediction models, which run on some of the world's most powerful supercomputers. The models divide the atmosphere into a three-dimensional grid and solve the equations of fluid dynamics and thermodynamics to project how it will evolve. Human forecasters then interpret the output, tempering it with local knowledge.

The gains have been striking. As a common rule of thumb, forecast skill has improved by roughly a day per decade, so a five-day outlook today is about as reliable as a one-day forecast was a few decades ago.

Yet there is a ceiling. The atmosphere is chaotic, meaning that imperceptible errors in the initial data amplify over time, the insight popularized as the butterfly effect. To cope, forecasters run ensembles of slightly varied simulations and express results as probabilities. Beyond roughly two weeks, day-to-day detail dissolves into noise.

Certification schemes and higher farm-gate prices are attempts to address these injustices, though their effectiveness is still debated.

paras: Few health messages are repeated as relentlessly as the claim that stress makes us ill. In her widely viewed TED talk, health psychologist Kelly McGonigal confesses that she spent years reinforcing that very message, only to be confronted by evidence that complicated it.

The turning point was a study that tracked roughly 30,000 American adults over eight years. High levels of stress were associated with a 43 percent greater risk of dying, yet this held true only for participants who also believed that stress was damaging to their health. A pounding heart and quickened breath can be reframed as signs that the body is mobilizing energy to meet a challenge, and people who learned to see stress this way showed a healthier response, with blood vessels that stayed relaxed.

She also highlights a less familiar side of the stress response: the release of oxytocin, a hormone that nudges us to seek and offer support. Seen in this light, stress is not merely something to be eliminated. Handled well, it can be a catalyst for courage and connection.

paras: Robert Waldinger directs the Harvard Study of Adult Development, which has followed people's lives for more than 80 years. In this later talk, he returns to the study's central finding: people with warmer relationships tend to be happier and healthier as they grow older.

c1.title: The Paradox of an Island Rich in Rain
c1.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 C1 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: Seen from space, Earth looks abundantly watery, yet the overwhelming majority of that water, about 97 percent, is saline. Of the small remainder that is fresh, most is locked in glaciers and ice caps or stored deep underground, leaving a strikingly thin margin readily available for human use.

Taiwan illustrates a paradox. Its annual rainfall is high by global standards, but the island's steep, short rivers rush much of that water to the sea within hours, and rainfall is concentrated in the plum-rain and typhoon seasons.

When typhoons failed to arrive in 2020, the island slid into one of its worst droughts in decades. By the following spring, reservoirs had dwindled to alarmingly low levels, prompting rationing in several regions and difficult trade-offs between farms, households and water-intensive industries.

Globally, agriculture accounts for the lion's share of freshwater withdrawals, which is why the most consequential savings often lie in efficient irrigation and leak-free distribution networks. Household habits matter too, but they work best alongside smarter infrastructure and pricing that reflects water's true scarcity.

paras: Penguins forfeited flight long ago, but evolution compensated generously. Their wings have hardened into rigid flippers, dense bones counteract buoyancy, and streamlined bodies slip through water with remarkable efficiency. Emperor penguins can descend more than 500 meters in pursuit of prey, holding their breath for many minutes.

Contrary to popular imagery, penguins are not exclusively creatures of the ice. Of roughly eighteen species, only a handful breed on Antarctica itself; the rest inhabit sub-Antarctic islands and the coasts of South America, southern Africa, Australia and New Zealand. One species even nests on the equatorial Galápagos.

The emperor penguin's breeding cycle is among the most grueling in nature. Through the Antarctic winter, males incubate a single egg on their feet, huddling together against ferocious winds and fasting for weeks until the females return from the sea.

That dependence on a stable environment leaves many species precarious. Shrinking sea ice threatens the platforms emperors need to raise chicks, while warming waters, overfishing and pollution disrupt the food webs on which all penguins rely.

paras: Paper is so ubiquitous that it has become almost invisible, yet for most of recorded history writing depended on far less convenient surfaces: clay tablets, bamboo strips, costly silk or parchment made from animal skin. Each constrained how much could be written and who could afford to do so.

The breakthrough came in China. Fragments of early paper predate him, but Cai Lun, an official of the Han court, is traditionally credited around 105 CE with refining a method of pulping plant fibers into thin, durable sheets.

The technique remained a closely held advantage for centuries before spreading westward along trade routes to the Islamic world, where paper mills flourished, and eventually to Europe. Paired with movable-type printing, abundant paper made books cheap enough to fuel mass literacy, the circulation of scientific ideas and the spread of religious and political debate.

The shift to wood pulp in the nineteenth century made paper cheaper still, at considerable cost to forests. Recycling now recovers much of what we use, though not indefinitely: each cycle shortens the fibers, which is why recycled paper typically requires an infusion of fresh pulp.

c1.title: The Practice of Social Fitness

source.name: TED：Robert Waldinger, The secret to a happy life: lessons from 8 decades of research

c1.note: 內容主題取自 TED 熱門演講。內文為學習用改寫，不是講者原話，請看原演講了解細節。
paras: Robert Waldinger has spent much of his career overseeing the Harvard Study of Adult Development, an investigation now spanning more than eight decades and, more recently, the children of its original participants. In this later talk, he revisits the study's most robust conclusion: the quality of our relationships is among the strongest predictors of health and happiness as we age.

What Waldinger adds here is a practical metaphor. Relationships, he suggests, behave like muscles. Neglect them and they atrophy; tend to them and they strengthen. Just as we accept that physical fitness requires ongoing effort, he argues that we should cultivate what he calls social fitness.

The framing is deliberately modest. Rather than demanding grand gestures, he points to small acts sustained over time: rekindling a lapsed friendship, asking a coworker a question that invites a genuine answer, giving someone our undivided attention.

Part of the talk's appeal is that it counters a pervasive myth, namely that connection should happen effortlessly. Waldinger's research suggests the opposite: lasting bonds are maintained deliberately, and it is never too late to begin.
